answer.exemplar: Each frame appends to the same list object, and an append is visible to every other frame the instant it happens, so a level that resumes after its branches return finds not only what it added but everything its descendants added. Sharing is not wrong in itself, it is right when the caller wants one progressively built result, and it is the wrong choice when each level needs its own view of the output.

answer.exemplar: The loop inside the method is not what fixes the order; the call structure is. A recursive call does not return until its whole subtree is finished, so the stack holds one root-to-node path and nothing else, and there is no place in it to keep the siblings that were discovered but not yet reported. A level order needs exactly that: every node found at the current depth, held until the whole depth is reported. A queue supplies the missing structure, because it releases the oldest discovered node first, so all nodes at one depth leave before any node at the next. The recursive form would have to be rebuilt as a loop over that queue, and once it is, the recursion has no work left to do, which is why the order and the control structure are not separable.

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by the call structure, not by the loop inside the method. A recursive call does not return until its entire subtree is finished, so the stack holds one root-to-node path and has nowhere to keep the siblings that have been discovered but not yet reported. A level order needs exactly those pending nodes held together, so the first node discovered is the first one reported, which is the definition of a queue. Building a recursive version of that walk means giving each frame a sibling list, and the moment a frame has to pass such a list down, the method is a loop over a queue with extra steps. That is why the order and the control structure cannot be separated, and why a recursive rewrite can only ever return to depth-first order.

answer.exemplar: Write down the measure you are prepared to defend, then check each branch separately and only that. A termination proof is a claim about every path, so one bad branch invalidates it no matter how good the other branch is, and the fastest way to find the bad branch is to compare the argument each one passes against the argument that branch received. In a grid walk where the second call decrements the row index while the guard tests the last row, the row distance grows instead of shrinking, so that branch alone is enough to produce an unbounded chain of frames. The confirming evidence is not a message but a run: instrument a counter and the count climbs until the stack is exhausted, and repairing only that one branch makes the run terminate with a finite count.
